rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥā Mīm is the Qur’anic name of the sūra, and the sūras named Ḥā Mīm share common subjects.
rows.anchor: all sūrahs which are named ﺣٰﻢٓ have common subjects.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Ḥā Mīm could be read as the inchoative with the next sentence as its enunciative, he prefers an independent sentence with an omitted inchoative.
rows.anchor: ﺣٰﻢٓ is an independent sentence whose inchoative is suppressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also takes the inchoative of “a revelation from the Compassionate, the Merciful” to be suppressed, yielding “The Qur’an is a revelation” from God.
rows.anchor: The translation keeping in view this suppression would be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He relates this construction to the similar wording at 40:2 and says the following verse clarifies it by calling the revelation a book whose verses are explained.
rows.anchor: In the previous sūrah, it was similarly said thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanzīl conveys thoroughness, diligence, and majesty: God revealed the book thoroughly and grandly through an elaborate arrangement.
rows.anchor: it expresses thoroughness, diligence and majesty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm show that divine mercy motivated the Qur’an’s elaborate revelation; he connects this to God teaching the Qur’an in 55:1–2.
rows.anchor: it is God’s attribute of mercy which is responsible for the revelation of the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mercy names sharpen the rebuke: the rejecters refuse a great mercy and demand the punishment it warns about, a theme developed in what follows.
rows.anchor: to pinpoint the horrendous nature of the denial of these people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads this as the second enunciative and a further account of God’s favor: an Arabic Qur’an makes the message easy for its Arab audience and preempts a complaint that revelation was not in their language.
rows.anchor: the second enunciative after the first and a detail of the mercy and favour of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In li-qawmin the verb implies intention: the arrangement benefits people who intend to know and understand, while those without that intention gain nothing.
rows.anchor: made all this elaborate arrangement for those who intend to know and understand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He urges the Arabs to seek knowledge because they had received no earlier divine scripture and God was now teaching them through a book in their own language.
rows.anchor: it was the first time that the Almighty out of His mercy revealed to them His book in their own language

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is both bearer of glad tidings for those who accept it, promising success in this world and the next, and a warning of dreadful torment for rejecters; it must not be taken lightly.
rows.anchor: For those who accept it are glad tidings of success both in this world and in that to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people treat the Qur’an as ordinary and evade listening or understanding, failing to recognize it as a divine warning rather than an ordinary sermon.
rows.anchor: are not ready to listen to or understand it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse details the disbelievers’ arrogant evasion of the Prophet and his companions: they claim their hearts are closed to the call and it has not affected them.
rows.anchor: This verse mentions the detail of the evasion shown by the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He compares their claim of closed hearts with the Jews’ parallel claim in the Qur’an at 2:88.
rows.anchor: This comment is the same as the one the Jews would make.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says “listening” is omitted after wa, with the parallel clause indicating the ellipsis.
rows.anchor: points to this suppression. I have translated this verse keeping in view this aspect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied meaning is that their ears are deaf to the Qur’an being recited to them.
rows.anchor: Our ears are blind to the Qur’ ān you are reading out to us.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barrier between the parties denotes a wide gulf in their beliefs, ideologies, and religion, leaving no prospect of closeness.
rows.anchor: a great gulf of beliefs, ideologies and religion separates them from the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given this gulf and lack of communication, each side is told to act as it chooses; in the context of the earlier warning, “do what you will” alludes to the opponents’ demand that punishment be brought.
rows.anchor: demand of punishment these enemies used to make.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verses answer, through the Prophet, the demand implicit in the opponents’ “do what you will.”
rows.anchor: These verses give an answer through the tongue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is a human being, not God, and has no authority to bring punishment at their demand; that authority belongs to God.
rows.anchor: he is not God so that he is able to bring the punishment at their demand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since their Lord is one with no partner, they must devote themselves wholly to Him, seek forgiveness for their past polytheism, and turn back to their true Lord.
rows.anchor: their Lord is one; no one is His partner or associate; so they should fully devote themselves to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Destruction awaits polytheists who do not spend in God’s cause and rely on alleged intercessors rather than fear God; they are the real rejecters of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: devastation awaits all the polytheists who do not spend in the way of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh here means spending in God’s cause generally, a usage current in the Makkan period; after a specified form was prescribed in Madinah, the term came to denote it, but here it retains its earlier general sense.
rows.anchor: This word is used to convey this meaning in the Makkan period as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer’s overall point is that the Prophet cannot bring the threatened punishment, while the opponents are warned that polytheists relying on deities and intercessors face destruction.
rows.anchor: only God has this authority; however, his opponents must stand warned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the inchoative in the statement about the Hereafter adds emphasis, making the sense “it is only they who are its rejecters.”
rows.anchor: has incorporated a special emphasis in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their profession of belief in the Hereafter is invalid if they think partners or intercessors can win salvation for them regardless of their deeds; they are its true rejecters.
rows.anchor: cannot be regarded as believers of the Hereafter; in fact, they are its real rejecters.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their polytheistic view negates the divine justice and wisdom on which the Hereafter rests.
rows.anchor: these people have totally negated God’s justice and wisdom on which the Hereafter is based.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike other Hereafter-deniers, who regard it as far-fetched or doubt it, these people undermine the very rationale of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Others who have rejected the Hereafter have rejected because they think that it is far-fetched

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following verses call polytheism disbelief because it negates God’s primary attributes, leaving no real difference between belief in God and disbelief in Him.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān has clearly called polytheism as disbelief.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 8 contrasts the preceding warning with glad tidings: those who embrace faith and do righteous deeds receive an eternal reward.
rows.anchor: However, those who embraced faith and did righteous deeds, for them is an eternal reward.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads ghayr mamnūn as an unending reward; although others interpret the expression differently, the Qur’anic parallel at 11:108 supports his reading of favors that never cease.
rows.anchor: the parallels of the Qur’ ān reinforce my interpretation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 9–12 direct attention to God’s power, providence, wisdom, and oneness in the heavens and earth; verse 12 summarizes the argument, which he will discuss verse by verse before summarizing and addressing objections.
rows.anchor: This topic is spread over four verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflection on the world rules out self-origination, mere amusement, or a battleground of rival gods; it points instead to the planning and wisdom of an all-powerful, all-knowing God.
rows.anchor: it has come into being on account of the planning and wisdom of the all powerful and all knowing God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Quraysh’s idolaters did not deny God, the Qur’an calls their polytheism disbelief: valid belief must affirm God’s attributes, rights, and their implications, and denying any attributes makes belief unacceptable.
rows.anchor: the verse addresses the idolaters of the Quraysh who never denied God yet the Qur’ ān has regarded their polytheism as disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an explicitly addresses idolaters as disbelievers, as at 109:1.
rows.anchor: Proclaim: “O you Disbelievers!” (109:1)).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects taking the “two days” for the earth’s creation as two earthly days; he says they mean another kind of days, without completing the explanation in this excerpt.
rows.anchor: do not mean two earth days as has been explained at an appropriate place
